title: Can ChatGPT Play the Role of a Teaching Assistant in an Introductory Programming Course?
venue: Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE 2024)
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether ChatGPT can function as a virtual teaching assistant in an introductory programming (CS1) course. The authors focus on two core TA responsibilities: grading student code submissions and providing feedback on student code. The motivating problem is that large introductory programming courses require many human TAs, which creates workload and consistency challenges in grading and feedback.

The study evaluates OpenAI's GPT-3.5 model (text-davinci-003) using data from three take-home Python programming assignments. For grading, the authors compare ChatGPT's functionality scores against scores previously assigned by human TAs for 6,783 student code submissions. They also ask ChatGPT to assess code quality and compare those judgments with code quality metrics computed using the Radon package, especially Halstead effort and modularity. For feedback, they sample around 10 submissions per assignment, ask ChatGPT to generate improvement suggestions, and evaluate these suggestions both subjectively through expert student reviewers and objectively by implementing the suggestions and recalculating code quality metrics.

The population consisted of first-year undergraduate students in a CS1 course at IIIT Delhi in India, with the course enrolling approximately 650 students and supported by 32 highly proficient TAs. The context was a single institutional setting in which Python was the programming language of instruction. In addition to the student submissions, four strong undergraduate reviewers with TA experience evaluated the quality of ChatGPT-generated feedback.

The main conclusions are mixed. ChatGPT was not reliable enough to replace human TAs for grading: its correctness scores showed substantial deviation from TA scores, and its code quality judgments correlated weakly with tool-generated quality metrics. However, ChatGPT performed better as a feedback generator: most of its comments were judged to be minor or critical improvement suggestions rather than erroneous, and incorporating its suggestions often improved modularity and code structure, though not code correctness. The authors conclude that ChatGPT shows promise for instructional support and feedback, but is not yet dependable for grading student code submissions.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family conversational large language model used here as a virtual teaching assistant for programming coursework.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a TA-like system in an introductory programming course to grade Python code submissions for correctness and quality, and to generate feedback/suggestions for improving student code.

findings.finding_summary: For grading code correctness, ChatGPT's scores showed substantial deviation from human TA grading across three assignments. Overall mean deviation was 5.35/20 for Assignment 1 with correlation 0.143, 5.47/16 for Assignment 2 with correlation 0.462, and 3.94/10 for Assignment 3 with correlation 0.59; the authors conclude ChatGPT was not reliable enough for grading correctness.
findings.measure: Deviation and Pearson correlation between ChatGPT-assigned functionality scores and TA-assigned scores on programming assignments

findings.finding_summary: For code quality grading, ChatGPT's assigned quality scores had near-zero correlation with Radon-derived quality metrics. Correlations with Halstead effort were -0.024, -0.04, and 0.16 across Assignments 1-3, and correlations with modularity were -0.012, 0.054, and 0.19, indicating poor alignment with computed code quality measures.
findings.measure: Pearson correlation between ChatGPT-assigned code quality scores and Radon package metrics (Halstead effort, modularity)

findings.finding_summary: In subjective evaluation of generated feedback, most comments were judged useful rather than erroneous. Across assignments, 70.77%-76.19% of comments were classified as minor enhancement feedback, 21.43%-21.65% as critical improvement feedback, and only 2.38%-4.62% as erroneous; four expert student reviewers performed the classification.
findings.measure: Reviewer classification of ChatGPT feedback into minor enhancement, critical improvement, erroneous, or none
findings.sample_size: n=4 reviewers; approximately 10 submissions sampled from each assignment

findings.finding_summary: When ChatGPT's suggestions were implemented, code modularity improved while correctness changed minimally. Average new/old modularity ratios were 1.12 for Assignment 1, 1.11 for Assignment 2, and 1.49 for Assignment 3, while effort-score ratios were 0.93, 1.33, and 0.93 respectively; the authors report no significant improvement in code correctness.
findings.measure: Ratio of modified-to-original code quality metrics after implementing ChatGPT feedback; regraded correctness of modified code

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical primary study with a clear experimental design and large archival dataset for grading comparisons, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental impact evaluation of student outcomes. Parts of the feedback analysis also rely on small samples and subjective review.
impact_tier_rationale: Findings are mixed: ChatGPT performed poorly as a grader but showed useful feedback-generation potential, mainly improving code modularity rather than correctness. Reported effects are correlational/ratio-based and do not establish clear learning gains.
